approved: Argued in support of the Paid Parental Leave Amendment Bill 2014 as a way to cut red tape for small business, and warned that Australia's fertility rate has fallen from 3.5 births per woman in 1963, when he was born, to 1.87 today, below the replacement rate.

Argued against the Paid Parental Leave Amendment Bill 2014, tracing how the coalition's own scheme's projected cost shifted from $2.7 billion to $8.8 billion and then to $5.5 billion, and said this policy drift undermines the government's claim to competent economic management.

Argued in support of the Paid Parental Leave Amendment Bill 2014, said employers administering the scheme costs businesses about $48 million a year nationally, including nearly $14.4 million in New South Wales in the 2012 to 2013 financial year, and noted Labor had twice voted the same amendment down while in government.

Argued against the Paid Parental Leave Amendment Bill 2014, said eighty per cent of women of child-bearing age in his Charlton electorate earn under $42,000 and would receive $29,000 less under the coalition's scheme than a millionaire would, calling the policy fundamentally inequitable.

Argued in support of the Paid Parental Leave Amendment Bill 2014, said removing employers from administering the scheme would save businesses $44 million a year and the not-for-profit sector $4 million a year, and cited a business survey in which 84.3 per cent of respondents agreed employers should not act as government paymasters.

Argued against the Paid Parental Leave Amendment Bill 2014, said the coalition's broader scheme would give $50,000 to a woman earning $100,000 or more, while a woman on the minimum wage would receive only $16,000, calling this a demonstration of the government's skewed budget priorities.

Defended the Paid Parental Leave Amendment Bill as saving businesses $44 million a year and the not-for-profit sector $4 million, with $11.67 million of that saving in Victoria alone, citing an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry survey showing 84 per cent of businesses want employers relieved of the paymaster role.

Defended the bill's $44 million savings for small business, said the share of Australians employed in small business fell from 53 per cent under the Howard government to 43 per cent under Labor after 519,000 small business jobs were lost in six years, and argued a woman earning the average full-time salary would be about $50,000 better off in retirement under the coalition's paid parental leave scheme than Labor's.

Cited an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry survey finding 84.3 per cent of businesses opposed employers acting as paymaster for paid parental leave, and said the bill would shift an estimated $44 million in business costs onto government administration for about $7 million.

Opposed the bill, cited a survey in which 54 per cent of employers disagreed that administering paid parental leave was time-consuming, quoted business leaders including Innes Willox saying the current system works well, and said Labor's scheme has benefited 340,000 families with a median recipient income of $45,000, compared with the coalition's scheme costing $5.5 billion a year.

Supported the bill as reducing red tape for small business, cited savings of $44 million a year for business and $4 million for the not-for-profit sector nationally, with New South Wales alone expected to save over $14 million, and traced the amendment's history back to a private member's bill voted down by Labor on 24 February 2011.

Opposed the bill returning Paid Parental Leave administration from employers to Centrelink, arguing the Productivity Commission had recommended employer administration specifically to preserve workforce attachment, cited estimates that losing an employee can cost a business around $70,000, and criticised the Prime Minister's separate scheme for paying $50,000 to uncapped high earners after only lowering its threshold from $150,000 to $100,000.

Defended the Paid Parental Leave scheme as an equity measure for low and middle income women funded by a levy on big business, said it includes superannuation and extends leave to 26 weeks compared with Labor's 18, and cited feminist commentator Eva Cox's support for the coalition's scheme.

Clarified that the bill before the House is not the Abbott government's flagship Paid Parental Leave scheme itself, which has not yet been finalised or included in the budget despite being a core election promise.

Argued in support of the Paid Parental Leave Amendment Bill removing the employer paymaster role, estimating compliance savings of up to $48 million annually, and cited an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry survey in which 84½ per cent of 1,700 businesses agreed employers should not be paymasters for the $662-a-week, 40-day scheme.

Argued in support of removing the paid parental leave paymaster role from business, citing an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry survey where 84 per cent of businesses opposed the requirement, an average implementation cost of $1,783 per employer, and total savings of $44 million for business and $4 million for the non-profit sector.

Opposed the Paid Parental Leave Amendment Bill, citing a University of Queensland survey of 501 employers finding 74 per cent found the scheme easy to implement, noted 340,000 families have benefited from Labor's scheme after 55 per cent of working mothers previously had no access to paid leave, and said the coalition's alternative would cost more than $21 billion over the forward estimates.

Argued in support of the bill removing the paid parental leave paymaster burden from small business, citing an APEC Women and the Economy Forum finding that limits on female workforce participation cost member economies at least $89 billion a year, and said lifting Australia's female participation to the OECD average could add over $10 billion to GDP while closing an $87,000 superannuation gap between men and women.

Argued in support of the bill, citing an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry finding that 84.3 per cent of businesses opposed being paymasters for the scheme, criticised Labor's $9,700 taxed maternity payment as potentially leaving some women worse off, and noted Sweden pays parental leave for 68 weeks compared with Australia's 18.

Argued against the paid parental leave scheme's priorities, noting Australia did not appoint its first female federal cabinet minister until 1949, that female enrolment in formal study rose from about 17 per cent in 2001 to 20 per cent in 2013, and criticised a $450 million cut to out-of-school-hours care that would have funded extra places at over 500 schools.

Argued in support of the bill from personal experience as a former small business owner, recalling that administering $1,200-a-fortnight paid parental leave payments for two staff in 2011 took about 20 hours of research to set up, costing the business an estimated $750 to $1,000.

Argued against the extravagant paid parental leave scheme, contrasting it with his electorate's average family income of $55,000 a year, and asked why a wealthy solicitor's baby should attract more government support than the child of a low-income cleaner.

Argued that the member for Fairfax made a cowardly, wrong and ignorant allegation suggesting the Prime Minister's chief of staff Peta Credlin influenced the paid parental leave policy for personal benefit, and said attacking staff who cannot defend themselves is off limits in parliament.
